newsitem.title: USA: All but one weapon in FBI van found.
newsitem.headline: All but one weapon in FBI van found.

text.p: Federal officials said on Thursday they had recovered all but one weapon taken when an FBI van was stolen and looted and said there is no evidence the thieves knew what the vehicle was or what it contained.
"Nothing in the investigation indicates the (van) was stolen because it was an FBI vehicle," John Hancock, special agent in charge of the Memphis Division of the FBI, told a news conference.

He said the weapons -- including M-16s, a shotgun and rounds of ammunition -- were found in bushes, grass, under plywood and various other places in a neighbourhood on the north side of Memphis near where the van was found empty and burned earlier in the week.

The only weapon that was not recovered, he said, was an M-79 "gas delivery system" which can be used to fire tear gas or other types of shells. He also said there were no markings on the van identifying it as an FBI vehicle.

Veronica Coleman, the U.S. attorney for Memphis, said no charges have been filed in the case. Five people who may have seen or have other knowledge of the van theft were being questioned, Memphis police said earlier.

Hancock said it was "absolutely untrue" that the FBI assault team from Little Rock, Arkansas, to whom the van belonged had been reassigned. Coleman said an inquiry into how the theft happened was continuing.
The team was one of several in Memphis for a regional training exercise. The van was stolen from a motel parking lot.
FBI Director Louis Freeh had announced the weapons recovery earlier in Washington during an appearance before the House Judiciary subcommittee on crime.
Freeh was pressured by one member of the panel to fire or suspend the "knucklehead" FBI agents who left the van full of weapons unattended.

"Is this comic strip time or something?" asked Representative John Conyers, a Michigan Democrat who urged Freeh to suspend or fire the agents involved in order "to send a message to any other knuckleheads out there."

Freeh told the committee he wanted to be fair to the agents involved and "get all the facts together" before dismissing or suspending anybody. "This is a very serious matter. If we don't have rules and regulations, we will very quickly," he said.

Some members of the panel called on Attorney General Janet Reno to investigate the FBI's policies on weapons handling, asking incredulously how a SWAT van without special locks or an alarm system and full of sophisticated weapons could be left unattended in a hotel parking lot.
Tennessee Democratic Representative Harold Ford said the incident raised serious questions about the FBI's procedures.
"I find it extremely troubling that a mistake of this magnitude would ever occur. In light of this apparent negligence, a thorough investigation of this matter is warranted," he said.
Reno expressed concern about the incident at her weekly Justice Department news conference. "I'm troubled when an FBI van is stolen and weapons are taken and the FBI van is destroyed," she said.

"The FBI is reviewing all the processes and procedures in place to see what must be done to address this problem," she said. "We're reviewing it to see what happened, to see if we need to impose new procedures or to take other action."
